title: In 1752, Britain went to bed on 2 September and woke on the 14th
body: The old Julian calendar added a leap day every fourth year, so its average year of 365¼ days ran about **11 minutes** longer than the solar year. Over the centuries those minutes added up: in 1582 Pope Gregory XIII’s reform dropped 10 days and stopped leap days in century years not divisible by 400. Britain kept the old calendar until 1752, when the gap had grown to 11 days, so Wednesday 2 September was followed by Thursday 14 September. Tales of mobs demanding ‘give us our eleven days’ are very likely a myth.

slides.question: In the Gregorian calendar we use today, how many years in every 400 are leap years?
slides.explanation: 97. Years divisible by 4 are leap years, except century years that don’t divide by 400: 1600 and 2000 were leap years, 1700, 1800 and 1900 weren’t. That makes the average year 365.2425 days.

slides.alt: Animation on a printed almanac page: September 1752 with only 19 days, a leap-year cycle averaging 365¼ days, the spring equinox sliding from 21 to 11 March by 1582, the century leap-year rule, and days 3 to 13 dropping out of the month.
slides.music: “Brandenburg Concerto No. 4 in G, Movement I (Allegro), BWV 1049” Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com) · CC BY 4.0

slides.prompt: Run the Julian calendar on from AD 325 and watch the spring equinox drift; then switch to the Gregorian rule.
slides.takeaway: A Julian year is 11 minutes too long, so by 1582 the equinox had slid from 21 to 11 March. Dropping 3 leap days every 400 years slows the drift to about a day in 3,000 years.

slides.heading: Rent days moved too
slides.text: The Act moved rent days, salaries and contracts on by 11 days, so that nobody gained or lost. The quarter day of 25 March became 5 April, which is why the UK personal tax year still ends on 5 April.

slides.heading: New Year moved as well
slides.text: The same Act moved the start of the legal year in England from 25 March to 1 January. Scotland had already begun its year on 1 January since 1600.

slides.question: What do historians make of the tales of mobs shouting ‘give us our eleven days’?
slides.explanation: Very likely a myth. It rests on just two sources, a satirical journal and a satirical painting by Hogarth, and the riot records of the time show no such events.

slides.question: When did Russia switch to the Gregorian calendar?
slides.explanation: 1918. By then the jump was 13 days, because 1800 and 1900 had been leap years in the old calendar but not in the new one.
